Stephen was one of seven men appointed to oversee the daily distribution of food in the Jerusalem church, but Acts portrays him above all as a Spirit-filled preacher and worker of signs. A Greek-speaking Jew, he provoked opposition among Hellenistic synagogues in Jerusalem, was charged with speaking against the temple and the law, and delivered a long speech before the Sanhedrin that retold Israel's history as a story of God's presence beyond the temple and the people's resistance to his messengers.

He was stoned to death, praying for his killers and committing his spirit to Jesus in words that mirror Luke's account of the crucifixion. His death is a hinge in Acts: it introduces Saul of Tarsus, triggers the persecution that scatters the church beyond Jerusalem, and sets in motion the mission to Samaria and the Gentiles.

The church has honored him since antiquity as the protomartyr, the first to die for Christ, and his speech remains one of the most studied texts in Acts for what it says about the temple, the law and early Christian readings of Israel's scriptures.
30665: Acts names Stephen first among the Seven and says he was full of faith, the Spirit, grace and power, performed wonders and signs, and out-argued opponents from several diaspora synagogues. False witnesses accused him of saying Jesus would destroy the temple and change Mosaic customs. He gave a long speech (Acts 7), saw Jesus standing at God's right hand, and was stoned while Saul watched approvingly. The text does not call him a deacon; the noun is not used of the Seven, though the related verb (to serve tables) is.

Paul, also called Saul, was a Pharisee from Tarsus who persecuted the earliest followers of Jesus and then, after an encounter with the risen Christ near Damascus, became the most influential missionary and theologian of the first generation of the church. A Roman citizen at home in both Jewish and Greek worlds, he spent some three decades founding communities of Jews and Gentiles across Asia Minor, Macedonia and Greece, supporting himself by tentmaking and staying in touch with his churches through letters.

Thirteen New Testament letters bear his name. Seven are accepted by virtually all scholars (Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, Philemon); the authorship of the others is debated. These letters, the earliest Christian writings we have, argue that in Jesus's death and resurrection God has fulfilled his promises to Israel and opened his people to the nations, so that Gentiles belong by faith and the Spirit without becoming Jews through circumcision. Acts devotes more than half its length to him and narrates three missionary journeys, his arrest in Jerusalem, two years in custody at Caesarea and a perilous voyage to Rome.

Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome. Early Christian tradition, beginning with 1 Clement, holds that he was executed there under Nero. His reading of the gospel has shaped every major theological movement in the West, from Augustine to Luther to the New Perspective, and remains contested between traditions.
30821: Paul calls himself a Hebrew of Hebrews from the tribe of Benjamin, circumcised on the eighth day, a Pharisee, blameless under the law, and a former persecutor (Phil 3:5-6). Acts adds that he was born in Tarsus, a Roman citizen from birth, raised in Jerusalem under Gamaliel, and a tentmaker. He says he saw the risen Lord and was called as apostle to the Gentiles (Gal 1:15-16; 1 Cor 15:8). He lists beatings, three shipwrecks, a stoning, hunger and danger (2 Cor 11:23-28), and a thorn in the flesh he asked to have removed (2 Cor 12:7-9). He hoped to visit Rome and go on to Spain (Rom 15:24). Acts ends with him preaching in Rome under guard; no biblical text records his death, though 2 Tim 4:6-8 presents him as expecting it.
30822: Paul is the great apostle alongside Peter; together they are the founders of the Roman church, sharing a feast on 29 June. Justification is read as God's making the sinner truly righteous through grace received in baptism and lived out in faith working through love (Gal 5:6). Paul's letters are read within the tradition and teaching office of the church.
30823: Paul is honored as equal of the apostles and read through the Greek Fathers, especially John Chrysostom. Emphasis falls on union with Christ, participation in his death and resurrection, and theosis, with justification one facet of salvation rather than its organizing center.
30824: Paul's letters, especially Romans and Galatians, are the clearest statement of the gospel: sinners are justified by grace alone through faith alone on account of Christ's righteousness imputed to them, apart from works of the law. Luther's and Calvin's commentaries made this the hinge of the Reformation.

30826: Second Temple Judaism was not a religion of earning salvation but of covenantal grace. Critics respond that Paul also opposes human achievement in general (Rom 4:4-5); defenders reply that they do not deny this, only that it is not the main front.

30828: Paul never left Judaism; he remained a law-observant Jew whose mission was to bring Gentiles to Israel's God without making them Jews.
